learning_outcomes.description: Analyse, Evaluate, and Create Conflict Management Strategies in HWIs:Analyse the three levels of conflict and the corresponding management processes, critically evaluate existing strategies, and create innovative solutions for complex human-wildlife conflicts, integrating multidisciplinary approaches and stakeholder perspectives.

Analyse, Evaluate, and Create Stakeholder Engagement Strategies in HWIs:Analyse the systemic properties of human-wildlife interactions and the different conflict levels, critically evaluate existing engagement strategies, and create innovative, integrative solutions to foster coexistence through effective stakeholder engagement and negotiation processes.

Evaluate and Synthesise Knowledge in HWIs:Critically evaluate the role of various types of knowledge in human-wildlife interactions, synthesise insights to understand the politicisation of knowledge, and create strategies that leverage expert involvement to manage and mitigate conflicts effectively.

Analyse, Evaluate, and Create Financial Incentive Strategies for Conservation:Analyse the effectiveness of various financial incentives in promoting management of human-wildlife interactions on private land, critically evaluate existing economic tools and policies, and create innovative strategies to enhance the economic viability of conservation efforts while ensuring ecological and social sustainability.

Analyse, Evaluate, and Create Policy Frameworks in Human-Wildlife Conflict Management:Analyse the effectiveness of various policy instruments in managing human-wildlife conflicts, critically evaluate existing policies and their implementation, and create innovative policy recommendations to enhance the coexistence of humans and wildlife while ensuring ecological sustainability.

Analyse, Evaluate, and Create Evaluation Frameworks for Human-Wildlife Interaction Management:Analyse the effectiveness of various evaluation techniques in human-wildlife interaction management, critically evaluate existing evaluation frameworks, and create innovative evaluation plans that include comprehensive indicators, data collection methods, and analysis techniques to enhance the effectiveness of management strategies.

Integrate and appraise advanced multidisciplinary knowledge: Develop and lead sophisticated management strategies that integrate ecological, social, and economic disciplines, ensuring ethical, sustainable, and effective solutions to complex human-wildlife conflicts.

assessments.assessment_title: Essay on a human-wildlife interaction topic
assessments.task_description:
Students will write a 2,500-word essay (excluding the reference list but including in-text citations) on one of four topics related to human–wildlife interactions. The essay topics will be released during the semester.

The aim of this assessment is to develop a coherent, well-supported argument that demonstrates critical engagement with the chosen topic. Students are expected to move beyond describing course content by analysing and evaluating different perspectives, identifying strengths and limitations of existing approaches, and synthesising evidence from the literature to support their conclusions.

A list of recommended readings will be provided for each essay topic. Students are expected to draw on at least ten scholarly sources from the recommended reading list and may incorporate additional scholarly literature identified through their own independent research. There is no maximum number of references; however, assessment will focus on the quality of engagement with the literature rather than the quantity of citations.

Successful essays will:

  • develop a clear and well-structured line of argument;
  • critically engage with the relevant literature rather than simply describing it;
  • integrate evidence from scholarly sources to support claims;
  • demonstrate independent thinking and synthesis of ideas; and
  • be written in a clear, concise, and logical manner.

Acknowledging and/or referencing AI use 

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly acknowledge (by assessment coversheet) any use of AI or MT in each instance.  

A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.  

The use of AI or MT must be acknowledged appropriately. Please see assessment guidelines in blackboard course site for specific instructions. Students may also refer to Library guides found under Additional assessment information > Acknowledging and referencing AI use.

assessments.task_description:
This assessment requires students to participate in a multi-stakeholder mediation simulation focused on a fictionalized human–wildlife conflict in Belize. Students will be assigned stakeholder roles and participate in a facilitated Townhall-style negotiation and mediation process. The simulation is designed to expose students to the complexity of conservation conflicts involving competing values, identities, livelihoods, governance priorities, conservation objectives, and social tensions.

These sequential assessment components intertwine with the mediation simulation assessment.

Conflict systems analysis

Due: Prior to the mediation simulation

Length: ~1,000 words (individual)

Students will prepare an individual conflict systems analysis of the human–wildlife conflict. The submission consists of a written analysis and a conflict systems map. Drawing on the simulation materials, academic literature, and relevant course concepts, students will analyse the relationships between stakeholders, their interests, values, needs, and sources of influence, as well as the social, ecological, institutional, and governance factors shaping the conflict. Students will identify opportunities and barriers for collaboration and consider implications for the design of an effective mediation process.

Acknowledging and/or referencing AI use  

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly acknowledge any use of AI or MT in each instance.  

A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.  

The use of AI or MT must be acknowledged appropriately. Please see assessment guidelines in blackboard course site for specific instructions. Students may also refer to Library guides found under Additional assessment information > Acknowledging and referencing AI use. 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Designing a conflict management strategy

Due: After the mediation simulation

Length: ~1,500 words (individual)

Following the simulation, students will prepare a conflict management strategy for the Belize Council. The report should evaluate the townhall mediation as one step in a broader conflict management process and provide recommendations for future engagement.

Students may consider questions such as:

  • What was achieved through the townhall process?
  • Which issues remain unresolved and why?
  • Which conflict level(s) remain and what does this imply for future intervention?
  • Is further negotiation appropriate, or is mediation, reconciliation or institutional reform now required?
  • What additional stakeholder engagement activities would you recommend?
  • Which stakeholders should be involved in future processes?
  • How should different knowledge systems be incorporated?
  • What governance or policy changes could support long-term coexistence?
  • What should happen over the next 12 months?

Students should support their strategy using relevant course concepts and academic literature.

A failure to acknowledge generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.

Students must participate in the simulation to receive a mark for this assessment task.

This assessment task is not eligible for re-mark because it is completed live during the scheduled class activity and cannot be replicated after the event. Due to the structure of the assessment, recording student performance is not possible. As there is insufficient reviewable evidence to reconsider the original assessment judgement, students cannot apply for a re-mark. 

Mediation Simulation Participation

Students will participate in class in a facilitated multi-stakeholder mediation simulation involving negotiation, dialogue, conflict management, and media engagement. Students are expected to actively represent the perspectives, interests, and concerns of their assigned stakeholder group while engaging constructively with other participants.

The simulation will involve:

  • stakeholder caucus discussions,
  • negotiation and mediation processes,
  • responses to escalating tensions,
  • engagement with contested evidence and competing narratives,
  • and interaction with media representatives.


This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct.
